title: MAC Addresses, ARP and Switches
oneLiner: How a frame actually reaches the device next to you: MAC addresses, the ARP question "who has this IP?", and a switch learning which port each device is on.
keyTakeaway: IP addresses say where a packet is going overall; MAC addresses say which device on this local network gets the frame next. ARP finds the MAC address for an IP on the same network by broadcasting a question, and a switch learns which port each MAC lives on from the frames it sees, so after the first exchange it sends frames only where they need to go.
explanation:
Every network card has a MAC address (Media Access Control address), 48 bits written as six hex pairs like 02:00:00:00:00:0b. It's the address Ethernet and Wi-Fi use for delivery within one local network. IP addresses are for getting across networks; MAC addresses are for the last step on each one. A packet keeps the same source and destination IP addresses all the way, but it is wrapped in a new Ethernet frame, with new MAC addresses, at every hop.

So before a PC can send anything to 10.1.1.20 on its own subnet, it needs that device's MAC address. ARP (the Address Resolution Protocol) gets it: the PC broadcasts "who has 10.1.1.20? Tell 10.1.1.10" to every device on the network, and only the owner replies with its MAC address. The answer goes in the ARP cache for a few minutes so the question isn't asked for every packet. For destinations on other networks the PC asks for its default gateway's MAC instead, as covered in Routing and Default Gateways.

A switch connects the devices on a network. It reads the source MAC address of every frame that arrives and records which port it came in on, building a MAC address table. When a frame arrives for a MAC it knows, it sends it only out of that port; for a broadcast, or a MAC it hasn't learned yet, it floods the frame out of every other port. An old hub flooded everything, always; a switch quickly learns not to, which is why other devices don't see your traffic.

ARP has no authentication: a device believes whatever reply it gets. ARP spoofing abuses that by sending fake replies ("the gateway is at my MAC") to sit in the middle of other people's traffic. Managed switches can block it with Dynamic ARP Inspection, and encryption such as TLS makes the intercepted traffic useless.
